newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian MTBE - Pace of recovery slow, arb wide open.
newsitem.headline: Asian MTBE - Pace of recovery slow, arb wide open.

text.p: Asian MTBE prices have edged up in the past week but industry sources said the rise is still lagging behind the hikes in Europe and the U.S. Gulf, leaving the arbitrage window wide open.
"Prices are up, but they are not even close to the European or U.S. Gulf values," a producer said.
"It is not quite the right pace but at least the direction is correct," he said.
A free-on-board (fob) Singapore MTBE parcel lifting in August traded earlier this week at $263 per tonne, pushing up assessments to around $263-$265 from $258-$260 last week, sources said.
Prices in the U.S. have been on the rise for more than three consecutive weeks as prompt barrels dried up amid news of plant turnarounds and octane demand.
Traders said this left the arbitrage window to the U.S. wide open at up $290 fob Singapore.
But they did not expect prices in Asia to soar by over $30 as its upside was was being capped by the bearish Asian gasoline market.
Benchmark 95-octane unleaded gasoline prices in Singapore have in the past week lost around 50 cents per barrel, hovering around the $23.00 mark.

Sources, however, still saw Asian prices rising due to a combination of fresh demand from oil majors, blenders and traders seeking cargoes for the U.S. and some shutdowns in this region but mainly those in the U.S.
In the region, South Korean oil refiner Yukong Ltd 44510.KS plans to shut down its 6,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) MTBE plant August 2-September 10.
It is closing the plant which is supplied with butane from an associated 50,000-bpd residue fluid catalytic cracker (RFCC) which is being shut for maintenance.
The Yukong shutdown should cut South Korean MTBE exports which have dried up on strong domestic demand over the peak summer months are due to re-emerge in August and September.
Spot export cargoes are also expected from Malaysia in September as regional producer MTBE Malaysia plans to optimise its output in August, sources said.
"It is not really because of better MTBE prices, although they have improved," a source said. "It is because propylene has fallen by around $200 per tonne to the high $400s in the past two months."

MTBE Malaysia, a wholly owned subsidiary of state-owned Petronas, produces 300,000 tonnes of MTBE and 80,000 tonnes of propylene annually from its plant at Kuantan on the east coast of the peninsular.
But the plant can vary the output of each product from between 100 percent to 80 percent of capacity depending on market conditions.
The source said the plant has been at "high-propylene" mode since the begining of the year.
